units.title: Thiazides: Site, Drug Groups and Metabolism
units.sec: Thiazides: Site, Drug Groups and Metabolism · p106
units.guide: Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule. Based on metabolism they are divided into drugs with minimal metabolism that are excreted unchanged - chlorothiazide, polythiazide and bendroflumethiazide (all with 100% oral bioavailability), chlorthalidone (the longest acting, over 24 hours, and the thiazide of choice in HTN) and metolazone (most potent, effective even below GFR 40, and DOC in mild to moderate HTN with renal insufficiency) - and drugs with maximal metabolism and minimal renal excretion such as indapamide.

units.title: Thiazides: Mechanism of Action
units.guide: Thiazides block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. The reduced Na+/Cl- reabsorption lowers osmotic pressure (raising uric acid and glucose reabsorption and causing dyslipidemia), delivers Na+/Cl- to the collecting duct (increasing Mg2+, H+ and K+ excretion via the H+ ATPase and ROMK pumps) and lowers intracellular Na+, which activates the Na+/Ca2+ antiporter and increases Ca2+ reabsorption. Thiazides also open K+ channels in smooth muscle, giving direct vasodilation.

units.title: Thiazides: Effects, Uses and Side Effects
units.sec: Thiazides: Effects, Uses and Side Effects · p107
units.guide: Thiazides produce moderate diuresis through a moderate (about 5%) loss of Na+/Cl- and water. They are DOC in HTN with edema of renal or hepatic origin, are ineffective at GFR below 40 (except metolazone), and can cause erectile dysfunction from volume depletion, while in HTN with CKD without edema the DOC changes to ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Direct vasodilation lets them serve as a first-line drug in HTN, and indapamide lowers the chance of erectile dysfunction because of less diuresis. Increased Ca2+ reabsorption causes hypercalcemia and makes them DOC in HTN with osteoporosis and useful in hypercalciuric renal stones, while effects shared with loop diuretics include hyperuricemia with gout, hyperglycemia worsening diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and metabolic alkalosis.

units.title: Potassium-sparing Diuretics: Drugs and Mechanism
units.sec: Potassium-sparing Diuretics: Drugs and Mechanism · p107
units.guide: Potassium-sparing diuretics are divided into ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene) and aldosterone receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, finrenone). Blocking ENaC lowers Na+/H2O reabsorption by only 1-3% so diuresis is poor; the fall in intracellular Na+ then lowers activity of the H+ ATPase (H+ excretion falls, H+ rises in the body) and of ROMK (K+ excretion falls, K+ rises in the body). Thus they cause poor diuresis with potassium sparing, so they are combined with other diuretics to prevent hypokalemia, and they retain H+ (metabolic acidosis) and K+ (hyperkalemia).

units.title: Aldosterone Receptor Blockers: Spironolactone, Eplerenone and Finrenone
units.sec: Aldosterone Receptor Blockers: Spironolactone, Eplerenone and Finrenone · p108
units.guide: Aldosterone receptor blockers are the only diuretics that do not act via the tubular lumen. Spironolactone is a prodrug whose active component is canrenone; it is DOC in cirrhotic edema and in resistant edema and HTN unresponsive to loop and thiazide diuretics. Its side effects come from receptor blockade: progesterone receptor blockade causes menstrual irregularities and testosterone receptor blockade causes gynecomastia and impotence, for which it is used as a second-line drug for hirsutism in PCOS (DOC: OCPs). Eplerenone is DOC in cirrhotic edema without the side effects of spironolactone, and finrenone is a new drug used in CHF with DM that lowers cardiovascular mortality in CHF/MI.

units.title: ENaC Blockers: Amiloride and Triamterene
units.sec: ENaC Blockers: Amiloride and Triamterene · p109
units.guide: Amiloride is DOC in lithium-induced diabetes insipidus (because Li+ is reabsorbed by ENaC), Liddle syndrome (ENaC overexpression) and cystic fibrosis. The page also notes that thiazides are used in lithium-induced and nephrogenic DI: the pure water loss of DI plus a thiazide leads to loss of Na+ with water, which triggers reabsorption of both water and Na+ by the PCT. Triamterene is used to treat edema and its side effect is folic acid deficiency, which contraindicates it in liver cirrhosis.

units.title: Mannitol
units.guide: Mannitol is listed with the loop diuretics. It is given IV for diuresis and orally for constipation. At the cellular level it extracts water into the systemic circulation, and at the organ level in the kidneys it causes solute free water loss. Its uses are DOC in acute congestive glaucoma, breaking diuretic resistance, bronchial challenge testing with the inhaled powdered form, DOC in cerebral edema and head trauma with raised ICP, and dialysis disequilibrium (aggressive diuresis lowers osmotic pressure and causes cerebral edema); it is used before expected or impending renal failure but is contraindicated in pre-existing renal failure, and it serves as the non-hemolytic irrigation fluid in transurethral resection of the prostate.

units.title: Free Water Clearance and the Effect of Diuretics on FWC
units.sec: Free Water Clearance and the Effect of Diuretics on FWC · p110
units.guide: In the thick ascending loop and distal convoluted tubule, Na+/Cl- reabsorption creates medullary hyperosmolarity and gives a positive free water clearance: solute is reabsorbed while water stays in the lumen. In the collecting duct, water moves through aquaporins under vasopressin acting on V2 receptors to give a negative free water clearance, meaning reabsorption of water only. Diuretics modify these: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors leave Na+ reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb and increase positive FWC; loop diuretics stop TAL Na+ reabsorption, lowering medullary hyperosmolarity and decreasing both positive and negative FWC; thiazides decrease reabsorption in the DCT and lower positive FWC.

units.title: Vasopressin Receptor Drugs: Analogues and Antagonists
units.sec: Vasopressin Receptor Drugs: Analogues and Antagonists · p111
units.guide: Vasopressin comes from the hypothalamus and acts on V2 receptors in the medullary collecting duct to move water, while Na+ movement in the TAL creates medullary hyperosmolarity. Vasopressin antagonists (conivaptan, mozavaptan, tolvaptan) are used in SIADH where endogenous vasopressin is increased, and vasopressin analogues (vasopressin, terlipressin, desmopressin) are used in central DI where endogenous vasopressin is decreased. Recombinant vasopressin acts on V1 (Gq) receptors in blood vessels to cause vasoconstriction - used in norepinephrine resistant shock and acute variceal bleed with facial pallor as a side effect - and in the GIT to cause contraction - used in paralytic ileus and abdominal distention with abdominal cramps; on V2 (Gs) receptors it treats central DI. Terlipressin is DOC in acute variceal bleed and the only drug to lower mortality (alternative: octreotide), and desmopressin is DOC for central DI, nocturnal enuresis, von Willebrand disease and hemophilia A.

units.title: Vasopressin Antagonists and Management of SIADH
units.sec: Vasopressin Antagonists and Management of SIADH · p112
units.guide: Vasopressin antagonists are used in SIADH: conivaptan is given intravenously in emergencies, and for maintenance/long-term oral therapy tolvaptan (limited to one month because of hepatotoxicity) or mozavaptan are used. SIADH is managed acutely by severity: mild cases get free water restriction with sodium tablets, while moderate cases (lethargy, confusion) and severe cases (seizures) get hypertonic saline. Long-term maintenance is free water restriction with or without sodium tablets.

units.title: Diuretics: Summary Table
units.guide: The summary table places each diuretic class with its target: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act on PCT carbonic anhydrase (acetazolamide, used in acute mountain sickness, causing renal stones, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, sulfonamide hypersensitivity and hyperammonemia that contraindicates them in liver cirrhosis), loop diuretics block Na+/K+/2Cl- in the thick ascending loop (furosemide, DOC in pulmonary edema, and if GFR is below 40 loops remain DOC with metolazone added if there is no response), thiazides block Na+/Cl- in the DCT (chlorthalidone, first-line in HTN, increasing Ca2+ so they are used in HTN with osteoporosis), potassium-sparing diuretics act on aldosterone receptors or ENaC (spironolactone DOC in cirrhotic edema causing gynecomastia; amiloride DOC in lithium-induced DI) and mannitol acts on loop more than PCT (DOC in cerebral edema, acute congestive glaucoma and diuretic disequilibrium).
